1.0.0.en: And Solomon the son of David was strengthened in his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him, and magnified him exceedingly. [1]

1.0.1.en: In the last chapter of First Chronicles it was said: “And the LORD magnified Solomon exceedingly in the sight of all Israel, and bestowed upon him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel” (1 Chr 29:25).

1.1.0.en: The Lord says: “Them that honour me I will honour” (1 Sam 2:30). Solomon honored the Lord; he gave priority to the Lord. Before he sat on the throne to carry out any kingly work concerning the nation, he gathered all the leaders and the people and went to the high place at Gibeon to offer a sacrifice to the Lord at the tabernacle of God which Moses the servant of the Lord made in the wilderness [3].

1.1.1.en: He received a throne that was contested by his brothers, but the Lord strengthened and magnified him, because He was with him.

1.1.2.en: In this book Solomon appears in wealth, greatness, authority and glory from the beginning of his enthronement, without stressing his increase in these things as the Book of Kings does. For this book presents Solomon to us as a type of the Lord Christ, who came down to carry humanity to His heavens and to grant them fellowship in the glories. If in His humility He became poor, it was only to enrich us by His poverty; His glories are not outside Him, rather He is the source of riches, righteousness, holiness and glory, and He desires to give us Himself, so that we may see in Him all sufficiency.

1.1.3.en: v There is none good but one, that is, God, who alone also brings happiness to man, and gives him peace, stability and tranquility[1].

1.1.4.en: St. Basil the Great v In honoring God we honor ourselves. He who opens his eyes to look at the light of the sun receives joy in it... Those who honor God do this for their salvation and for their great benefit; how? Because he who follows virtue glorifies God... Let us glorify God and bear Him in our bodies and our spirits (1 Cor 6:20)[2].

1.2.0.en: 2 Then Solomon spake unto all Israel, to the captains of thousands and of hundreds, and to the judges, and to every governor in all Israel, the chief of the fathers. 3 So Solomon, and all the congregation with him, went to the high place that was at Gibeon; for there was the tabernacle of the congregation of God, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness. 4 But the ark of God had David brought up from Kirjathjearim to the place which David had prepared for it: for he had pitched a tent for it at Jerusalem.

1.2.1.en: Then Solomon spake unto all Israel, to the captains of thousands and of hundreds, and to the judges, and to every governor in all Israel, the chief of the fathers [2]

1.2.2.en: It is clear that those around Solomon in positions of leadership were lovers of worship, so they shared with Solomon his love for communal devotional life.

1.3.0.en: So Solomon, and all the congregation with him, went to the high place that was at Gibeon; for there was the tabernacle of the congregation of God, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness. [3]

1.3.1.en: Gibeon was at one time the greatest sanctuary in Israel; by then it had become merely a station on the road to Jerusalem. The defects that spoil the beauty of Gibeon as a center of worship are not mentioned (1 Kgs 3:3-4). There is the tent of meeting, the tent of God which Moses the servant of the Lord made in the wilderness... and the bronze altar which Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, made, and he put it before the tabernacle of the Lord (2 Chr 1:3-5).

1.3.2.en: All the children of Israel gathered around King Solomon, and it describes here his journey with all Israel to Gibeon. The book mentions here details that are not found in the Book of Kings [3-6], to state that what Solomon does comes as an extension of what Moses did of old. The king wanted to affirm his sanctification and esteem of the tent of meeting which Moses the prophet had set up about 300 years earlier, and of the bronze altar that Bezaleel made (Ex 31:2-4; 38:22-31). So the building of Solomon's temple does not mean the destruction of the worship that Israel inherited; rather it is an extension of it, bearing the same thought[3].

1.3.3.en: Solomon began his reign with a popular visit to the tent of meeting and the altar of the Lord. It was a good opening to his work, as everyone felt the need for God's presence in their midst, and for their own presence in the house of the Lord, and indeed for the Lord to be in their company throughout the journey of their life.

1.4.0.en: But the ark of God had David brought up from Kirjathjearim to the place which David had prepared for it: for he had pitched a tent for it at Jerusalem. [4]

1.5.0.en: 5 Moreover the brasen altar, that Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, had made, he put before the tabernacle of the LORD: and Solomon and the congregation sought unto it. 6 And Solomon went up thither to the brasen altar before the LORD, which was at the tabernacle of the congregation, and offered a thousand burnt offerings upon it.

1.5.1.en: Moreover the brasen altar, that Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, had made, he put before the tabernacle of the LORD:

1.5.2.en: and Solomon and the congregation sought unto it. [5]

1.5.3.en: The secret of the power of the tent is the altar, which points to the Cross and the sacrifice of the Lord Christ for the salvation of the world. Through the Cross we bear the righteousness of the Crucified, and so we become righteous in the eyes of God. With this we sing, saying: “For the eyes of the Lord are over the righteous, and his ears are open unto their prayers: but the face of the Lord is against them that do evil” (1 Pet 3:12).

1.5.4.en: The going of the leaders and the people with Solomon to Gibeon, where the tent of meeting and the altar were, signifies our accompanying the crucified Lord Christ, the King of Peace, that we may enjoy the heavenly dwelling and experience the Cross, the power of God unto salvation (Rom 1:16).

1.6.0.en: And Solomon went up thither to the brasen altar before the LORD, which was at the tabernacle of the congregation, and offered a thousand burnt offerings upon it. [6]

1.6.1.en: Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on the altar [6], and perhaps more than that of peace offerings, a sign of joy and gladness before the Lord.

1.6.2.en: At the beginning of his account of Solomon, the writer stressed that he offered a thousand burnt offerings on the bronze altar, and when God appeared to Solomon He said to him: “I have chosen this place to myself for an house of sacrifice” (2 Chr 7:12). If the number 1000 in the Bible often points to heaven and the heavenly things, then this book, which concentrated on the temple and worship, aims to proclaim the opening of the gates of heaven to the Jews as well as to the Gentiles, so that the Church of the New Testament, which embraces everyone, may offer the sacrifice of the perfect burnt offering, that is, perfect love for God, just as Abraham offered his beloved son as an acceptable burnt offering and a pleasing aroma before God.

1.6.3.en: Some scholars observe that Chronicles does not mention the sin offering or the trespass offering, so that the altar appears as though it had been dedicated to burnt offerings and peace offerings. The building of the house of the Lord is a call addressed to all humanity to rise and share with the heavenly ones the sacrifices of praise, thanksgiving and glorification, as an expression of love and response to God's surpassing love for His rational creation.

1.6.4.en: While St. Ignatius was rejoicing in the Spirit on his way to martyrdom, he expressed his view of the Church as the surrendered Body of Christ; for Christ offers the Eucharist, His Body and Blood given up, so that the Church may live, enjoying with her crucified Bridegroom the spirit of self-giving. This is what led him to define the Church as the “place of sacrifice, Thysiasterion” in more than one place[4].

1.6.5.en: v May God increase you in riches; be gracious with these gifts to those who regard them and desire them, for I am a priest of my Lord Jesus Christ and to Him I offer the sacrifice every day, and I wish to offer my life as a sacrifice, as He offered His life as a sacrifice out of love for me[5].

1.7.0.en: 7 In that night did God appear unto Solomon, and said unto him, Ask what I shall give thee. 8 And Solomon said unto God, Thou hast shewed great mercy unto David my father, and hast made me to reign in his stead. 9 Now, O LORD God, let thy promise unto David my father be established: for thou hast made me king over a people like the dust of the earth in multitude.

1.7.1.en: In that night did God appear unto Solomon, and said unto him, Ask what I shall give thee. [7]

1.7.2.en: Since Solomon took care to speak with the leaders in a spirit of love, and set out with them to the tent of meeting, and offered a thousand burnt offerings on the altar, the Lord appeared to him, asking him about his needs.

1.7.3.en: Most likely the prophets Nathan and Gad were counselors to David the prophet and king, but it seems that there was no prophet in the days of Solomon, so the Lord Himself appeared to him and spoke with him. This does not mean that he was better than his father, with whom God spoke through His prophets, for God works by one means or another according to what the need requires. He spoke directly with some men of the Gentiles, such as Abimelech (Gen 20), and Pharaoh's Egyptian servants (Gen 40), and Pharaoh himself (Gen 41).

1.7.4.en: The word “ask” and its derivatives occur eight times in God's speech with Solomon here. For a man's request, especially from God, reveals to a great extent what is in his heart. If Solomon had been a warrior, he would have asked for victory over his enemies; but since he saw that he was a young leader who needed wisdom to manage the affairs of the people of God, and that he was the successor of the great king David, he therefore asked God for wisdom.

1.7.5.en: It is stated in Josephus, the Jewish historian, that when God appeared to Solomon, he leaped from his bed[6].

1.7.6.en: The Lord does not cease to ask us: “Hitherto have ye asked nothing in my name: ask, and ye shall receive, that your joy may be full” (Jn 16:24).

1.7.7.en: v What you ask is counted as nothing compared with what I want to give you. For what did you ask in my name? That the demons be subject to you. Do not rejoice in this, for what you have asked is nothing; for if that were something, He would be asking them to rejoice...

1.7.8.en: [That your joy may be full], that is, ask for what satisfies you.

1.7.9.en: When you ask for temporal things you ask for nothing. “Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again” (Jn 4:13)...

1.7.11.en: Speak in the language of Philip: [Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us] (Jn 14:8). [The Lord said to him: I have been with you all this time, and you have not known me? He who has seen me, Philip, has seen the Father also] (Jn 14:9) Vulgate.

1.7.12.en: Offer thanks to Christ, who became weak for your sake because you are weak, and let your desires be prepared for the divinity of Christ, that you may be satisfied by them[7].

1.8.0.en: v His saying “whatsoever ye have asked” must not be understood as any request whatever, but anything that truly bears on the blessed life. And what follows, “Hitherto have ye asked nothing in my name” (Jn 16:24), is understood in two ways: either you have not asked in my name, since you did not yet know my name as you ought, or you have asked nothing, if it is compared with what you ought to ask, so that what you ask is counted as nothing[8].

1.9.0.en: And Solomon said unto God, Thou hast shewed great mercy unto David my father, and hast made me to reign in his stead. [8]

1.9.1.en: A sense of gratitude with thanksgiving: “hast made me to reign in his stead”; You have placed me in the place of my father, the pious, righteous and great man, who completed his mission in a spirit of sincerity. It is as though he says, with Elisha to his spiritual father Elijah: [He gives me two portions of your spirit](*). Would that we carried the same spirit, so that we feel that the divine blessings our fathers received are an asset for us, which it befits us to enjoy.

1.9.2.en: His father David had received mercy from God, for although he sinned, through repentance he enjoyed the mercies of God.

1.10.0.en: v “No one is clean from defilement, even if his life is one day”[9]. David groans, saying: [In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother bore me] (Ps 51:5). The Apostle also declares: “For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood” (Rom 3:23-25). Therefore forgiveness of sins is granted to those who believe, since the Lord Himself said: “For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins” (Mt 26:28)[10].

1.11.0.en: St. Basil the Great v Although the servants of God and His friends avoid the sins that are unto death, and practice many good works, we do not believe that they are without trivial sins, for God does not lie when He says: [No child whose life is one day on the earth is without sin](**). Add to this the blessed John the Evangelist, who without doubt is no less than Job in worthiness, and who declares: [If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us] (1 Jn 1:8). Moreover, we read in another place: “For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again” (Prov 24:16)[11].

1.12.0.en: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles v You quoted the following statement from the Book of Job: [No one is clean, even if his age on earth is one day] (Job 4:14-5) LXX. And you added: “for we are guilty after the likeness of Adam's transgression[12]”, an opinion that your book on the prophecy of Jonah declares in an honorable and clear way, where you affirm that the little children of Nineveh were justly obliged to fast with the people merely because of their ancestral sins[13]. Therefore it is not improper for me to put the question to you: Where did the soul commit the iniquity from which it is obliged, even at this age, to be delivered by the mystery of Christian grace?[14]

1.13.0.en: v No man is without sin, whether his life is one day or he has lived many years. If even the stars are not pure in the sight of God(***), how much more the worm and the corruption into which those who were subjected to the sin of Adam's disobedience have fallen?[15]

1.14.0.en: Now, O LORD God, let thy promise unto David my father be established: for thou hast made me king over a people like the dust of the earth in multitude. [9]

1.14.1.en: “Let thy promise be established”: the best thing we ask of God is that He fulfill in us His divine promises to our fathers and to us, and to all humanity. “Remember the word unto thy servant, upon which thou hast caused me to hope” (Ps 119:49).

1.15.s.en: 5. Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge

1.15.0.en: Give me now wisdom and knowledge, that I may go out and come in before this people: for who can judge this thy people, that is so great? [10]

1.15.1.en: It is not mentioned here that he was a young lad who did not know how to go out or come in (1 Kgs 3:5-15), because he is a type of the Lord Christ, the wisdom of God. Rather it is said that he needed wisdom to go out and come in before the people and to judge them.

1.15.2.en: Solomon, as a true son of his father David, chose spiritual blessings, not temporal ones. Solomon knew that these gifts please God, and that He is the Giver of them (Prov 2:6).

1.15.3.en: “For who can judge this thy people, that is so great?” A beautiful sense of the weight and gravity of responsibility, together with confidence and certainty in God's possibilities and His gifts to us.

1.15.4.en: Solomon did not ask for wisdom in order to boast of it, but to serve the people of his Lord in a spirit of godliness, and to judge among them in a spirit of justice.

1.16.0.en: St. John Chrysostom says: [Since Solomon asked what ought to be asked, see how quickly he received. Two things must be in the one who prays: that he asks with zeal, and asks what ought to be asked[16].]

1.16.1.en: v David slept a peaceful death as though he were sleeping, and in his place came the boy Solomon to reign.

1.16.2.en: He (the Lord) said to him: [Keep my commandments as your father did, arise and rule over the kingdom of David your father.

1.16.3.en: Then I will be with you, and I will magnify your name in the world. If you are with me, you keep my commandments and do my will](****).

1.16.4.en: The boy knelt to pray before God, a pure prayer full of beauty to whoever contemplates it.

1.16.5.en: The virgin boy offered a pure prayer to the Lord, with words of love, and the Lord heard it in His exalted place.

1.16.6.en: O God of my father David, accept my prayer, and do not depart from me, for You have chosen me to become king.

1.16.7.en: Give me a heart full of the mysteries of hidden things, that I may judge Your people with faithfulness and righteousness (1 Kgs 3:7-9).

1.16.8.en: I am a boy, so be to me a chief teacher, wiser than any scribe, and guide the son of David, direct him and teach him, and give him wisdom.

1.16.9.en: I did not ask You for abundance of riches, but that I may know how to govern according to Your will (1 Kgs 3:9-11).

1.17.0.en: I did not ask, nor will I ask, for the souls of my enemies, but I ask only for a heart full of the mysteries of faith (1 Kgs 3:11)[17].

1.18.s.en: 6. God gives more than we ask

1.18.0.en: 11 And God said to Solomon, Because this was in thine heart, and thou hast not asked riches, wealth, or honour, nor the life of thine enemies, neither yet hast asked long life; but hast asked wisdom and knowledge for thyself, that thou mayest judge my people, over whom I have made thee king: 12 Wisdom and knowledge is granted unto thee; and I will give thee riches, and wealth, and honour, such as none of the kings have had that have been before thee, neither shall there any after thee have the like.

1.18.2.en: Because this was in thine heart, and thou hast not asked riches, wealth, or honour, nor the life of thine enemies, neither yet hast asked long life; but hast asked wisdom and knowledge for thyself, that thou mayest judge my people, over whom I have made thee king [11]

1.18.3.en: Where did this idea come from? If we return to (1 Chr 22:11-12), we hear the voice of David the prophet saying to his son: “Now, my son, the LORD be with thee; and prosper thou, and build the house of the LORD thy God, as he hath said of thee. Only the LORD give thee wisdom and understanding, and give thee charge concerning Israel, that thou mayest keep the law of the LORD thy God.” Solomon was listening to the voice of his father. Therefore, when the Lord asked him: “Ask what I shall give thee?” he immediately said: [I desire wisdom and knowledge] [11].

1.19.0.en: Wisdom and knowledge is granted unto thee; and I will give thee riches, and wealth, and honour, such as none of the kings have had that have been before thee, neither shall there any after thee have the like. [12]

1.19.1.en: God gave him riches, wealth and honor, although he did not ask for these things. Those who renounce the things of the world, the Lord gives them to them in abundance. The Lord Christ says: “Seek ye... the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you” (Mt 6:33).

1.19.2.en: He asked for himself wisdom or discernment, that is, he asked for practical wisdom through which he lives the life that befits a believer. God gave him intellectual and practical wisdom, so that there was none like Solomon until the Lord Christ came, who is greater than he (Mt 12:42; Lk 11:31). The Lord of glory Jesus promised us that if we seek the Kingdom of God and His righteousness, He will give us the other things, because they will not possess us or distract us from the Giver, nor corrupt our hearts (Mt 6:33). Together with heavenly grace He gives us our temporal needs, since all earthly goods become for our good; but without grace these goods enslave our souls.

1.19.3.en: v Then the Lord spoke with him, and said to him: I have chosen you, and I will not forsake helping you.

1.19.4.en: And because your mouth asked for righteous judgment (1 Kgs 3:13), and you hated wealth and empty glory, I will give you riches and glory with greatness, and your fame will spread everywhere and in the countries (1 Kgs 3:3).

1.19.5.en: And they will come on journeys, and see how great your wisdom is, and the report of you will spread among the kings and peoples of the earth, and every quarter will obey your fear[18].

1.20.s.en: 7. Solomon, his chariots and his horses

1.20.0.en: 13 Then Solomon came from his journey to the high place that was at Gibeon to Jerusalem, from before the tabernacle of the congregation, and reigned over Israel. 14 And Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen: and he had a thousand and four hundred chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen, which he placed in the chariot cities, and with the king at Jerusalem. 15 And the king made silver and gold at Jerusalem as plenteous as stones, and cedar trees made he as the sycomore trees that are in the vale for abundance. 16 And Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt, and linen yarn: the king's merchants received the linen yarn at a price. 17 And they fetched up, and brought forth out of Egypt a chariot for six hundred shekels of silver, and an horse for an hundred and fifty: and so brought they out horses for all the kings of the Hittites, and for the kings of Syria, by their means.

1.20.1.en: Then Solomon came from his journey to the high place that was at Gibeon to Jerusalem, from before the tabernacle of the congregation, and reigned over Israel. [13]

1.21.0.en: And Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen: and he had a thousand and four hundred chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen, which he placed in the chariot cities, and with the king at Jerusalem. [14]

1.21.1.en: The king was forbidden to multiply horses (Deut 17:16), lest he imitate the pagan kings who think that their greatness and glory lie in outward displays.

1.21.2.en: Solomon thrust himself into a forbidden arena, for his good father did not ride in a chariot, nor mount a horse; the most he mounted was a mule.

1.22.0.en: And the king made silver and gold at Jerusalem as plenteous as stones, and cedar trees made he as the sycomore trees that are in the vale for abundance. [15]

1.22.1.en: The book affirms that God fulfilled what He promised Solomon, giving him, together with wisdom, riches and glory. Solomon made gold and silver like stones, and cedar trees like the sycamore; the abundance of gold, silver and precious wood makes them cheap and lowers their value, whereas the abundance of grace increases its value.

1.23.0.en: And Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt,

1.23.1.en: and the king's merchants received the jalība at a price [16]

1.23.3.en: Jalība: some think that it means yarn or linen threads, for which Egypt was famous.

1.24.0.en: And they fetched up, and brought forth out of Egypt a chariot for six hundred shekels of silver, and an horse for an hundred and fifty: and so brought they out horses for all the kings of the Hittites, and for the kings of Syria, by their means. [17]

1.24.1.en: Solomon opened trade relations with Egypt, so he imported horses and linen, which he manufactured and exported to Syria at great profit (1 Kgs 10:28-29). Perhaps he learned that from his mother, who was like one of the virtuous women: “She makes garments and sells them, and delivers girdles to the Canaanite” (Prov 31:24).

1.24.2.en: Now everything was settled, and the situation was ready to begin the building of the temple.

1.24.3.en: In Your company I walk the royal road

1.24.4.en: v You were with Solomon, so he walked the royal road.

1.24.5.en: He was strengthened and learned much, because he clung to You.

1.24.6.en: With divine wisdom he did not work alone, but clung to all the leaders, not to show off his abilities, his knowledge and his wisdom,

1.24.7.en: but to set out with them to the tent of meeting.

1.24.8.en: And under Your shelter he enjoyed Your divine presence.

1.24.9.en: v Strengthen me, O my God, that I may walk the royal road.

1.24.10.en: I work with You, and in the shadow of Your grace.

1.24.11.en: I work with my brethren, and I do not separate myself from them!

1.24.12.en: In the midst of my brethren I meet You, O Lover of mankind!

1.24.13.en: v Would that You appear before me as You appeared to Solomon.

1.24.14.en: That I may hear Your divine voice, and so possess You!

1.24.15.en: In You and through You I enjoy divine wisdom.

1.24.16.en: You are the secret of my riches, my satisfaction and my joy.

1.24.17.en: You are the secret of my success and my happiness!

1.24.18.en: I hold fast to Your divine promises, as my fathers held fast to them.

1.24.19.en: v I walk in the royal road, and do not turn from it to the right or to the left.

1.24.20.en: I feel no want or need.

1.24.21.en: The silver of the world and its gold become like stones.

1.24.22.en: And the chariots of the world and all its possessions are as nothing.

1.24.23.en: v You lift my heart up to Your heavens.

1.24.24.en: And my soul is carried away as in a heavenly chariot.

1.24.25.en: I rest in You, and I am established forever.

1.24.26.en: The currents of the world do not terrify me.

1.24.27.en: And the trials of life do not break me.

1.24.28.en: I pass through all my life a joyful journey in Your company!

1.24.29.en: My soul is at peace, and the doors of my heart, my mind and my emotions open to You!

1.24.30.en: By Your cross You opened to me the gates of Paradise; by Your grace You open the gates of my inner man!

1.24.31.en: Enter, O King of kings, into my depths, and let Your Kingdom be established within me!
